paras: The attempted lynching of John Redd took place in October 1881 at Seale, Russell County, Alabama, when an armed crowd of several hundred tried to take Redd, a Black prisoner accused of murdering a Black woman, from the town jail. The sheriff and others persuaded the crowd to disperse, and although a wire dispatch passed on unconfirmed reports that Redd was later hanged, he was tried, found guilty of murder and sentenced to death in early November.

According to a dispatch datelined Decatur, Alabama, October 17, Redd was accused of choking to death a Black woman named Mary Ellis near Seale, carrying her body a quarter of a mile and throwing it into an old well. A Seale correspondent of the Columbus Times gave a different account, writing that a 'colored girl' had been found drowned in a well and that an examination showed 'the double crime of rape and murder.' A deputy sheriff found Redd hiding under fodder in an old fodder house and took him to jail.

The wire dispatch reported that 'an armed body of several hundred men' surrounded the jail in Seale at night and tried to take Redd out to lynch him. The sheriff and others talked them out of it 'for the time,' the dispatch said, adding that 'unconfirmed reports' had Redd taken out afterward and hanged.

The Columbus Times correspondent, writing on October 15, described the crowd differently: on the morning after the arrest, 'a regiment of colored men, backed by a battalion of white,' appeared behind a bugler. In that account the sheriff and a Colonel Waddell met the marchers before they reached the town and turned them back by 'persuasive powers.'

Redd was not lynched; a dispatch dated November 5 reported that he had been found guilty of murder and sentenced to death. No report of arrests or charges against members of the crowd was found in the coverage.

Northern papers carried the story as a crime brief, first as a short special in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer that mentioned only the murder. The Decatur dispatch ran in the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier under 'Lynch Law for a Murderer' and in the Omaha Daily Bee, whose deck announced the 'Lynching of the Murderer of a Colored Woman in Alabama Yesterday' on the strength of the unconfirmed rumor. Both called Redd the murderer outright and gave the crowd no racial description.

The Savannah Morning News, summarizing the Columbus Times letter among Georgia and Alabama news items, gave the more local version and credited the sheriff and Waddell with stopping the crowd. The conviction notice appeared in the Washington National Republican and the Dallas Herald in November, with no reference to the earlier lynching report.

The accounts differ on the crowd's makeup, on whether it reached the jail or was stopped outside town, and on timing, with the October 15 letter placing the crowd earlier than the wire's 'last night' of October 16. They also differ on the charge, choking in the wire and rape and murder in the local letter, which does not name the dead girl.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Redd
bases: An armed crowd of several hundred tried to take John Redd from the Seale jail (or was stopped on its way to town) to lynch him, but was turned back; he was later tried and sentenced to death (A2, A4, A5).

A crowd of several hundred tried to lynch Redd for an alleged murder but was dissuaded by the sheriff (A2, A4); the 'unconfirmed reports' of a later hanging (A2) are contradicted by November dispatches that he was found guilty and sentenced to death (A5, A6), so no killing occurred: an attempted lynching.

Two independent accounts, the Decatur wire dispatch (A2, A3) and the Seale correspondent's letter to the Columbus Times (A4), both report a large crowd turned back from lynching Redd, though they differ on details.

accounts.label: Wire report (Decatur, Oct. 17)
accounts.gist: Redd choked Mary Ellis and threw her body in a well; several hundred armed men surrounded the Seale jail at night and were dissuaded 'for the time' by the sheriff, though unconfirmed reports said he was later hanged.

accounts.label: Seale correspondent to the Columbus Times (Oct. 15)
accounts.gist: A colored girl was found drowned in a well, a victim of 'rape and murder'; Redd was jailed, and the next morning a crowd of colored men backed by whites, led by a bugler, was turned back before reaching town by the sheriff and Colonel Waddell.

accounts.label: Conviction dispatch (Nov. 5)
accounts.gist: Redd was found guilty of murder and sentenced to death.

framing.detail: Northern papers ran the Decatur dispatch under 'Lynch Law for a Murderer' and 'Lynching of the Murderer of a Colored Woman', calling Redd the murderer outright.
The Savannah Morning News summarized the Columbus Times letter as a state news item, crediting the 'persuasive powers' of the sheriff and Colonel Waddell.
